newsitem.title: GERMANY: Thyssen group net falls to 350 million marks.
newsitem.headline: Thyssen group net falls to 350 million marks.

text.p: Thyssen AG, Germany's largest steel maker, said on Friday group net profit fell to 350 million marks ($233 million) in 1995-96 from 775 million the year before, but it expects its results to improve gradually this fiscal year.
Pretax profit in 1995-96 fell to 654 million from 1.026 billion, while sales slipped to 38.7 billion from 39.1 billion.
Faced with sharp profit drops, Thyssen proposed a dividend cut to eight marks for the year ended September 30 from 10 marks the year before.
"In view of a light upward economic development, a gradually improving development of the Thyssen Group is expected," the company said in a statement.
It announced a major restructuring in the hopes of boosting profitability, and said it had already started to sharpen its focus and shed non-core businesses.
"The profit figure was a bit of a shock to the system, but the real question is what are the benefits and costs of the restructuring," said analyst Glen Liddy at Kleinwort Benson in London.

After extensive press speculation about the planned restructuring this week, the company's statement seemed short on details, which will probably be unveiled at the company's annual news conference on January, Liddy said.
Despite lower profits, Thyssen shares held up well as traders said the dividend cut was smaller than expected.
In after-hours trade on Friday, Thyssen shares fell to 273.50 marks from 274.60 the day before.
Thyssen said it would reorganize its industrial portfolio into five primary and five secondary profit centres, and divest itself of loss-making and non-core operations.
The core divisions will be elevator manufacturing, automotive components, flat steel production, production systems, and materials trading.
The "potential core business areas" were construction technology, real estate, industrial services, logistics and telecommunications.

Thyssen lost 220 million marks in 1995-96 in non-core businesses of little strategic importance, a spokesman said. Core businesses alone turned a profit of one billion marks on sales of 26 billion marks.
"This shows clearly the solid substance of the core activities," the spokesman said. Non-core business had sales of about five billion marks employing about 11,000 staff, he said.
Thyssen said the restructuring measures were fully reflected in its 1995-96 balance sheet. "This process is under way."
The supervisory board approved a 2.6 billion marks investment programme emphasising core businesses. Approved investments now in the pipeline stand at 4.3 billion marks.
In the year ended September 30, the company invested 2.4 billion marks, up from 2.2 billion the year before.
Thyssen said its steel unit Thyssen Stahl AG would build a thin-slab casting mill at a cost of 550 million marks in the German city of Duisburg.

The mill, the first of its type in Germany, would have capacity of 1.2 million tonnes per year. It would work together with Thyssen Stahl's two existing hot steel rolling mills in Duisburg and employ 170 workers.
The total group workforce stood at 122,659 on September 30, down from 126,444 a year earlier.
Steel division sales were 10.6 billion marks, and the division profit was considerable lower than the year before.

Capital goods sales rose to 12.7 billion marks and profit was generally higher. The trade and services division saw sales of 18.2 billion marks, just below the previous year's level, but profit was down sharply. --Bonn newsroom, 49 228 26097150 ($1=1.5021 Mark)
